newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts still see privatisation of Cr Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: Analysts still see privatisation of Cr Lyonnais.

text.p: France's new Socialist government is likely to go ahead with privatisation of state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais and insurer GAN despite election talk of halting selloffs, financial analysts said on Tuesday.
"I think their privatisation is inevitable," said one Paris analyst who did not wish to be named. "Otherwise they run the risk these companies could still cost the state money."

Both Credit Lyonnais, which nearly collapsed under the weight of a lending spree carried out when the Socialists were previously in power, and GAN, which was hard hit by a deep property slump, have cost the state billions of francs in aid.
The cost to taxpayers from Credit Lyonnais' runaway expansion is likely to exceed 100 billion francs ($17.2 billion) and could hit 150 billion, according to some estimates.
While Credit Lyonnais has staged an unexpectedly strong recovery, GAN still is not fully provisioned against its real estate losses, business daily Les Echos said on Tuesday.
The previous conservative government had already submitted a proposal to the European Commission to privatise GAN, that included plans for a 20 billion franc recapitalisation.

The sale of GAN, in which rival insurer AGF has expressed keen interest, was expected to take place this year. Ex-prime minister Alain Juppe had also said the sale of Credit Lyonnais, initially set for the end of 1998, could take place in 1997.
For the time being, the Socialists have put all sales on hold. During the election campaign, they pledged to keep public service companies under government control.

But they did not rule out all privatisations, saying they would take a "pragmatic approach" to state-controlled firms in the competitive sector which did not have a public service role and where state-control was no longer necessary.
"They have got enough of an escape clause there to give them the room to manoeuvre to decide to privatise," said a banking industry executive.
The shares of Credit Lyonnais and GAN have lost heavily in recent days on worries about their privatisation chances.
Credit Lyonnais was down 1.45 percent in afternoon trade at 204 francs while GAN was off 3.44 percent at 115.0 francs against an overall higher market.

"It is clear that in such public sector areas as defence, the Thomson-CSF sale for example, sales are going going to be stopped," said another Paris analyst. "But I think sales of financial companies will go ahead. There is no (public service) reason to keep them."

After numerous delays, the previous conservative government and Credit Lyonnais finally reached accord last month on a plan to privatise the bank but the government did not want to send it to the European Commission for clearance before the election.
The European Commission, which must approve all state aid, has said it will need around four months to evaluate the plan.
The bank has said it will need the Commission's green light by September in order to close its half-year accounts.

The bank needs the Commission's approval for a decision by the previous government to neutralise the cost of a loan granted by the bank under a previous state bailout to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.
"If the bank doesn't get approval, the cost of the loan would weigh heavily on its results," said the banking executive.
But the new Socialist administration will have to examine the plan before sending it to Brussels which could take time.

The banking executive said it was difficult to see how the plan, believed to involve disposal of most of the bank's European assets outside France to meet EU conditions for approval of state aid, could be changed in any substantive way. "Strategies have been decided, steps have been taken," he said.
While the CFDT union representing bank staff urged the government on Tuesday to abandon the planned privatisation, Credit Lyonnais' management favours the sale.
Its chairman Jean Peyrelevade has links to the Socialists as he was a top aid to former Socialist prime minister Pierre Mauroy between 1981 and 1983. ($ = 5.825 French Francs)
